title: The realm of truth
hookLine: Sach Khand is described as the home of the Formless, the goal of the path
tomorrow: The five realms as a path

cards: Near the end of Japji, the morning prayer, Guru Nanak describes a series of realms, khands, like rooms opening one into the next. Tomorrow walks the whole series. Today goes straight to the last room.
And something strange happens there. After stanza upon stanza of description, Guru Nanak stops and admits that describing this place is hard. Hard like iron.
The poet who has named worlds upon worlds reaches the realm of truth and says plainly that words strain here.

teach.h: SACH KHAND: THE REALM OF TRUTH.
teach.b: Sach is truth; khand is a realm, a region. Sach Khand, the realm of truth. You reached it once before, near the end of year one's walk through the Japji.
Japji says, in paraphrase: in the realm of truth dwells the Formless One, Nirankar. Creating, the One watches over the creation, and blesses it with the glance of grace.
That's nadar, the glance we met with the robe and the door. Here it isn't one look at one person. It's the One gazing on everything made, with joy.

The pauri says there are worlds there, and continents and universes beyond counting; try to count them, and there'd be no end. Form upon form, all moving as the hukam moves them, and the One sees them and is glad.
Here the week's threads meet: the order everything lives within, the grace that opens the door, the Formless One beyond and within.
Sikh readers take Sach Khand as the goal of the path, the home of the Formless.

teach.h: WORLDS BEYOND COUNTING, IN THE HUKAM.
teach.b: Some read it as a place the soul reaches; some as a state of union lived even now, which links it back to yesterday's free while living. Then the honest end.
In paraphrase: to describe this, Nanak says, is as hard as iron. The text holds the door open, and admits it can't fully describe the room.

how: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning, ending with the realms that lead to Sach Khand, the realm of truth where the Formless One dwells.

games.q: what does “the realm of truth” mean?
o: the home of the Formless One, watched with grace
a gurdwara court where Sikh disputes are settled
a heaven kept for those who never tell a lie

games.q: the realm of truth: tap the pairs.
p: how hard it is to describe

s: Guru Nanak describes Sach Khand in complete detail
he says describing it is as hard as iron.
Japji says the Formless One dwells in the realm of truth
creating, watching, blessing with the glance of grace.
Sach Khand can only be read as a place after death
some read it as a place the soul reaches, some as a state of union lived now.

games.q: you're a poet who has described realm after realm, and now you reach the last one, the realm of truth. what do you do?
o: describe it as confidently as all the others.
describe what you can, then admit words strain here.
skip it and end the poem early.
games.why: Guru Nanak describes the Formless One's home, then says describing it is as hard as iron.

practice: Let the words in your head slow down, the way the Guru's words slowed at the edge of this realm, and when a thought comes, let it pass without naming it.
If you pray, rest in being seen by a gracious glance; if you don't, rest in what's true right now: this breath, this room, nothing to add.

wordCard.voice: The realm of truth. Sach Khand, which Japji calls the home of the Formless One, where creation is watched with grace, and which Guru Nanak says is as hard as iron to describe. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sach Khand, the realm of truth, the home of the Formless.

carryVoice: Your line: home in truth. Some rooms are bigger than any words. See you tomorrow.
